In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 00396| 00397| Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. ---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

Done. View transitions implemented per the Next.js 16 guide (`node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/02-guides/view-transitions.md`), verified with a passing `next build` and smoke test.

**Shared element morph** — grid thumbnails and detail hero wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={\`product-${slug}\`} share="morph" default="none">` (app/ProductGrid.tsx:14, app/product/[slug]/page.tsx:57), with a 400ms morph + blur keyframe in globals.css.

**Directional navigation** — grid links tagged `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`, back link `['nav-back']`; both pages wrapped in a `ViewTransition` mapping types to `nav-forward`/`nav-back` enter/exit classes with ±60px slide CSS.

**Suspense reveals** — skeletons wrapped in `exit="slide-down"`, content in `enter="slide-up"` (both `default="none"`) on the home grid and product details.

**Reduced motion** — `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` zeroes all `::view-transition-*` animation durations/delays and disables the skeleton pulse.

Also added `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` to keep the page clickable mid-transition, and `types/react-canary.d.ts` (`import {} from 'react/canary'`) so `ViewTransition` typechecks against `@types/react`'s canary channel.
